newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Venezuelan "fuel from hell" takes on world.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Venezuelan "fuel from hell" takes on world.

text.p: Anyone who doubts the British adage "where there's muck, there's brass (money)" should go to Venezuela's Orinoco Tar Belt.

Using a deceptively simple process and new technology, Venezuelan oil engineers are turning huge reserves of sticky deposits into a fuel which, though dubbed by environmentalists the "world's filthiest", is winning markets around the globe.

"Many people, when they see it, just don't believe it," said Eleanor Morris, a process engineer with Bitumenes de Orinoco (Bitor), the state-owned company that produces and markets the trademark boiler fuel Orimulsion.
In the spotless lab of the Morichal processing plant, Morris demonstrated how the fuel is made by mixing bitumen with water in giant blenders.
As in all winning formulas, a secret ingredient -- a surfactant -- is added to enable the incompatible fluids to mix, creating an emulsion which can be burned in power stations.

Nearby, clusters of wells pump the gooey black tar out of the ground and send it along pipes to the processing station. The wells, which use the latest diagonal and horizontal drilling technology, stand among the pine trees of a long-established plantation. A handful of engineers maintain the wells and plants which are impeccably clean and atomized.
"People have called it the fuel from hell but this doesn't look like hell to me," said Eladio Bueno, Bitor's marketing and supply manager.
SLAMMED BY ENVIRONMENTALISTS
But for environmentalists, Orimulsion is the most toxic of all the hydrocarbon fuels.
"It's like heavy fuel oil except worse," said Max Wallis, research officer for Friends of the Earth Cymru, based in the Welsh capital Cardiff.
Friends of the Earth and other pressure groups are challenging British generator National Power's plans to modify an oil-fired plant in Pembroke, south Wales to burn Orimulsion.
Bitor attributes the aggressive campaign against the fuel to a combination of closed minds and political lobbying, particularly by the coal industry.
"There has been a pretty well organised campaign against the fuel," said one British power industry source who asked not to be named.
Compared with its chief competitor, Orimulsion emits 20 percent less carbon dioxide per BTU (British Thermal Unit) than coal and lower emissions of nitrogen oxide and particles, Bitor says.
Orimulsion's main handicap -- a high sulphur content of four percent -- can easily be brought within environmental limits with modern flue cleaning procedures, the company adds.
"There have been more studies on Orimulsion's impact on the environment than any other product. Some people just don't want to listen," Bueno said.
DISCOVERED BY CHANCE

Back in the sweltering savannah lands surrounding Morichal, 275 miles (440 km) southeast of Caracas, Bitor's emulsification process manager Claudio Ponte recalled how the state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) stumbled on the fuel in the mid-1980s.
"PDVSA wanted to transport some of this bitumen away from here so it mixed it with water," he said.
When tests were carried out on the mix they discovered its potential use as a combustible.
The first test shipments of Orimulsion started in 1988. Canada's New Brunswick Power station liked it so much it signed a 20-year contract for delivery of 700,000 tonnes a year.

Other contracts followed and last year Bitor exported 4.2 million tonnes of Orimulsion to five countries, including Japan, Denmark and Lithuania. Trials are being carried out in numerous others, including China which Bitor hopes will contribute to boost sales to as much as 32 million tonnes by 2005.
Private partners are queuing up to join Bitor in exploiting the fuel. U.S. oil giant Conoco, Norway's Statoil and Bitor are to start work on a $320 million processing plant later this year.
RESERVES PRACTICALLY LIMITLESS
There is no concern that such rapid growth will deplete reserves.

According to Bitor, Venezuela could export as much as 100 million tonnes of the fuel annually and still not run out for more than four centuries. "For practical purposes reserves are inexhaustible," Bueno said.
For PDVSA, Orimulsion forms part of an ambitious strategy to make use of the vast reserves of heavy oil found in the Orinoco Tar Belt.

According to PDVSA's Planning Coordinator David Escojido, the Orinoco belt contains about 1.2 trillion barrels of heavy oil in place. If only one fifth of this were recoverable Venezuela would easily surpass Saudi Arabia as the biggest oil province in the world.
FLORIDA CASE PENDING
Despite remarkable success in a short space of time Orimulsion was dealt a number of serious blows last year.
First, a U.S. state court blocked Florida Power and Light's plans to use four million tonnes per year of the fuel at its Mantee, Florida, plant.
Then, Britain's PowerGen Plc, one of Bitor's oldest and largest customers, announced it was closing down its Ince power station in northern England.
Florida Power and Light are appealing against the court's decision and PowerGen insists that the decision to close Ince had nothing to do with the fuel.
"The technical aspects of Orimulsion trials have been very successful," said a spokesman for PowerGen.
But environmentalists insist these cases are down to Orimulsion's poor pollution track record.
"In terms of hazardous particles, which are now recognised as the worst pollutant, it is the dirtiest fuel for our lungs," Wallis said.
The particles which plants burning Orimulsion emit are smaller in diameter than other fuels and thus more easily absorbed by humans and animals, he added.

Despite the environmental campaigns, the only successful case brought against Orimulsion-fired plants came in January last year when PowerGen reached an out of court settlement over a claim for damages arising from emissions from its Richborough power station in Kent, southern England. PowerGen said the damage to hundreds of cars in 1991 was caused by a fault at the plant.
